rewritten_text:
I met the strange man I am about to describe in Warwick Castle. Three things drew me to him: his open, straightforward manner, his astonishing knowledge of old armor, and the restful experience of his company, since he did all the talking. Like shy people often do, we found ourselves together at the back of the group touring the castle. He immediately began saying things that caught my interest. His conversation flowed softly and pleasantly. As he spoke, he seemed to drift out of our world and time into a distant age and a forgotten country. Gradually he cast such a spell over me that I felt surrounded by ancient ghosts, shadows, dust, and mold, talking to someone who belonged among them. He spoke of Sir Bedivere, Sir Bors de Ganis, Sir Launcelot of the Lake, Sir Galahad, and the other great knights of the Round Table just as I would speak of close friends, enemies, or familiar neighbors. And as he continued, he began to look impossibly old, faded, dry, and musty. Then he turned to me and asked as casually as if discussing the weather:

“You know about souls passing into other bodies. Have you heard of people exchanging ages—and bodies?”

I said I had not. He showed so little interest, as people do when discussing the weather, that he did not even notice whether I answered. A brief silence followed, broken almost immediately by the paid guide’s droning voice:

“Ancient chain-mail coat, sixth century, from the time of King Arthur and the Round Table. Said to have belonged to Sir Sagramor le Desirous. Notice the round hole over the left breast. No explanation for it. Thought to be a bullet hole made after firearms were invented, perhaps deliberately by Cromwell’s soldiers.”

My companion smiled, a smile that seemed to have fallen out of use many centuries ago, and apparently murmured to himself:

“Know this: I saw it happen.” After a pause, he added, “I did it myself.”

By the time I recovered from the shock, he had disappeared.

That evening I sat by the fire at the Warwick Arms, dreaming of ancient times while rain struck the windows and wind roared around the roof and corners. Now and then I opened old Sir Thomas Malory’s wonderful book, enjoying its feast of marvels and adventures, savoring its long-forgotten names, and sinking into dreams again.

We spent several miserable hours waiting until eleven, when the trial was due to begin. My father and the rest of the family had to appear as witnesses, and I went with them to court. Throughout that wretched imitation of justice, I endured a living torture. The question was whether my curiosity and reckless experiments would cause two deaths: one victim a smiling child, innocent and joyful, the other murdered still more terribly, under a burden of disgrace that would make the killing unforgettable in its horror. Justine was a worthy young woman, with qualities that should have ensured a happy life. Now everything would be buried in a shameful grave, and I would be responsible. A thousand times I would rather have confessed to the crime myself. But I had been absent when it occurred; such a confession would have been dismissed as a madman’s ravings and would not have cleared the woman suffering because of me.

Justine appeared calm. She wore mourning clothes, and the seriousness of her feelings made her always attractive face exquisitely beautiful. She seemed to draw confidence from her innocence and did not tremble, although thousands stared at her and cursed her. The spectators’ belief in the terrible crime she supposedly committed erased any sympathy her beauty might otherwise have inspired. Yet her composure was visibly forced. Her earlier confusion had been presented as evidence of guilt, so she made herself show courage. On entering the courtroom, she looked around and quickly found where we sat. A tear seemed to cloud her eye at the sight of us, but she soon regained control. Her expression of sorrowful affection seemed to declare her complete innocence.

The trial opened. After the prosecutor stated the charge, several witnesses were called. A number of strange circumstances worked against her, enough to shake anyone who lacked my certainty of her innocence. She had been out all night when the murder occurred. Near morning, a market woman had seen her close to the place where the child’s body was later discovered. Asked what she was doing there, she had looked very strange and given only a confused, incomprehensible reply. She reached the house at about eight. When someone asked where she had spent the night, she said she had been searching for the child and urgently asked whether there was any news of him.

The day went much like the one before. Mrs. Hurst and Miss Bingley spent several morning hours with the patient, who continued to recover, though slowly. In the evening Elizabeth joined the others in the drawing room. This time, however, there was no table set for loo. Mr. Darcy was writing, while Miss Bingley sat nearby watching his letter grow and repeatedly interrupting with messages for his sister. Mr. Hurst and Mr. Bingley played piquet, and Mrs. Hurst watched them.

Elizabeth picked up some needlework and found considerable amusement in listening to Darcy and his companion. Miss Bingley constantly praised his handwriting, his straight lines, or the length of his letter. His complete indifference to these compliments made their exchange curious and matched Elizabeth’s opinion of both of them exactly.

“Miss Darcy will be so pleased to receive a letter like that!”

He did not reply.

“You write remarkably quickly.”

“You’re mistaken. I write rather slowly.”

“You must have so many letters to write every year! Business letters too. I would find them dreadful.”

“Then it is fortunate that I have to write them and you don’t.”

“Please tell your sister how much I want to see her.”

“I have already told her once, at your request.”

“I’m afraid your pen isn’t pleasing you. Let me trim it. I’m exceptionally good at trimming pens.”

“Thank you, but I always do that myself.”

“How do you manage to write such even lines?”

He said nothing.

“Tell your sister how delighted I am to hear that her harp playing is improving. And please say that I absolutely adore her lovely little table design. I think it far better than Miss Grantley’s.”

“May I save your enthusiasm for my next letter? I don’t have room at present to do it justice.”

“Oh, it doesn’t matter. I’ll see her in January. But do you always write her such charming long letters, Mr. Darcy?”

“They are usually long. Whether they are always charming is not for me to decide.”

“I always say that anyone who can write a long letter easily cannot write badly.”

“That compliment won’t work on Darcy, Caroline,” her brother exclaimed. “He doesn’t write easily. He spends too long searching for four-syllable words. Don’t you, Darcy?”

“My writing style is very different from yours.”

“Oh,” cried Miss Bingley, “Charles writes as carelessly as anyone possibly could.
